communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Then it makes it the easier for me to propose that you should come away with me for a week to the Continent.

events.label: Holmes explains his unusual state and plans to leave London to pursue Moriarty

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There was something very strange in all this. It was not Holmes's nature to take an aimless holiday, and something about his pale, worn face told me that his nerves were at their highest tension. You have probably never heard of Professor Moriarty? Aye, there's the genius and the wonder of the thing! The man pervades London, and no one has heard of him. That's what puts him on a pinnacle in the records of crime. I tell you, Watson, in all seriousness, that if I could beat that man, if I could free society of him, I should feel that my own career had reached its summit, and I should be prepared to turn to some more placid line in life. Between ourselves, the recent cases in which I have been of assistance to the royal family of Scandinavia, and to the French republic, have left me in such a position that I could continue to live in the quiet fashion which is most congenial to me, and to concentrate my attention upon my chemical researches. But I could not rest, Watson, I could not sit quiet in my chair, if I thought that such a man as Professor Moriarty were walking the streets of London unchallenged.

events.label: Holmes describes Moriarty's career and background

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: What has he done, then? His career has been an extraordinary one. He is a man of good birth and excellent education, endowed by nature with a phenomenal mathematical faculty. At the age of twenty-one he wrote a treatise upon the Binomial Theorem, which has had a European vogue. On the strength of it he won the Mathematical Chair at one of our smaller universities, and had, to all appearances, a most brilliant career before him. But the man had hereditary tendencies of the most diabolical kind. A criminal strain ran in his blood, which, instead of being modified, was increased and rendered infinitely more dangerous by his extraordinary mental powers. Dark rumours gathered round him in the university town, and eventually he was compelled to resign his chair and to come down to London, where he set up as an Army coach. So much is known to the world, but what I am telling you now is what I have myself discovered.

events.label: Holmes states that he knows the higher criminal world of London and has followed a trail to Moriarty

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: As you are aware, Watson, there is no one who knows the higher criminal world of London so well as I do. For years past I have continually been conscious of some power behind the malefactor, some deep organizing power which forever stands in the way of the law, and throws its shield over the wrong-doer. Again and again in cases of the most varying sorts—forgery cases, robberies, murders—I have felt the presence of this force, and I have deduced its action in many of those undiscovered crimes in which I have not been personally consulted. For years I have endeavoured to break through the veil which shrouded it, and at last the time came when I seized my thread and followed it, until it led me, after a thousand cunning windings, to ex-Professor Moriarty of mathematical celebrity.

events.label: Holmes describes the Professor's criminal organization

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: He is the Napoleon of crime, Watson. He is the organizer of half that is evil and of nearly all that is undetected in this great city. He is a genius, a philosopher, an abstract thinker. He has a brain of the first order. He sits motionless, like a spider in the centre of its web, but that web has a thousand radiations, and he knows well every quiver of each of them. He does little himself. He only plans. But his agents are numerous and splendidly organized. Is there a crime to be done, a paper to be abstracted, we will say, a house to be rifled, a man to be removed—the word is passed to the Professor, the matter is organized and carried out. The agent may be caught. In that case money is found for his bail or his defence. But the central power which uses the agent is never caught—never so much as suspected.

events.label: Holmes says he devoted himself to exposing and breaking up the organization

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: This was the organization which I deduced, Watson, and which I devoted my whole energy to exposing and breaking up.

events.label: Holmes explains that evidence seemed impossible to obtain

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: But the Professor was fenced round with safeguards so cunningly devised that, do what I would, it seemed impossible to get evidence which would convict in a court of law.

events.label: Holmes compares Moriarty as an intellectual equal after three months

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You know my powers, my dear Watson, and yet at the end of three months I was forced to confess that I had at last met an antagonist who was my intellectual equal. My horror at his crimes was lost in my admiration at his skill.

events.label: Moriarty makes a trip and Holmes closes in
Holmes predicts the police will seize Moriarty and his gang in three days

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: In three days—that is to say, on Monday next—matters will be ripe, and the Professor, with all the principal members of his gang, will be in the hands of the police. Then will come the greatest criminal trial of the century, the clearing up of over forty mysteries, and the rope for all of them; but if we move at all prematurely, you understand, they may slip out of our hands even at the last moment.

events.label: Holmes says he could have succeeded without Moriarty's knowledge

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Now, if I could have done this without the knowledge of Professor Moriarty, all would have been well. But he was too wily for that.

events.label: Holmes says Moriarty observes his every step and tries to escape

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: He saw every step which I took to draw my toils round him. Again and again he strove to break away, but I as often headed him off. I tell you, my friend, that if a detailed account of that silent contest could be written, it would take its place as the most brilliant bit of thrust-and-parry work in the history of detection. Never have I risen to such a height, and never have I been so hard pressed by an opponent. He cut deep, and yet I just undercut him. This morning the last steps were taken, and three days only were wanted to complete the business.

events.label: Holmes sees Moriarty appear in his room
Holmes describes Moriarty's appearance

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: His appearance was quite familiar to me. He is extremely tall and thin, his forehead domes out in a white curve, and his two eyes are deeply sunken in his head. He is clean-shaven, pale, and ascetic-looking, retaining something of the professor in his features. His shoulders are rounded from much study, and his face protrudes forward, and is forever slowly oscillating from side to side in a curiously reptilian fashion. He peered at me with great curiosity in his puckered eyes.

events.label: Holmes remarks that the man has less frontal development than expected

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You have less frontal development than I should have expected.

communicates.speaker: professor_moriarty
communicates.content: You crossed my path on the 4th of January. On the 23rd you incommoded me; by the middle of February I was seriously inconvenienced by you; at the end of March I was absolutely hampered in my plans; and now, at the close of April, I find myself placed in such a position through your continual persecution that I am in positive danger of losing my liberty. The situation is becoming an impossible one.

events.label: Holmes asks whether the man has any suggestion to make

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: I asked. any suggestion to make?

events.label: The man tells Holmes to drop it and says he must withdraw

communicates.speaker: professor_moriarty
communicates.content: You must drop it, Mr. Holmes. You really must, you know. I am quite sure that a man of your intelligence will see that there can be but one outcome to this affair. It is necessary that you should withdraw. You have worked things in such a fashion that we have only one resource left. It has been an intellectual treat to me to see the way in which you have grappled with this affair, and I say, unaffectedly, that it would be a grief to me to be forced to take any extreme measure. You smile, sir, but I assure you that it really would.

events.label: Holmes says danger is part of his trade

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Danger is part of my trade.

events.label: The man says the situation is not danger but inevitable destruction

communicates.speaker: professor_moriarty
communicates.content: That is not danger. It is inevitable destruction. You stand in the way not merely of an individual, but of a mighty organization, the full extent of which you, with all your cleverness, have been unable to realize. You must stand clear, Mr. Holmes, or be trodden under foot.

events.label: Holmes says he is neglecting important business and rises to leave

communicates.speaker: professor_moriarty
communicates.content: Well, well. It seems a pity, but I have done what I could. I know every move of your game. You can do nothing before Monday. It has been a duel between you and me, Mr. Holmes. You hope to place me in the dock. I tell you that I will never stand in the dock. You hope to beat me. I tell you that you will never beat me. If you are clever enough to bring destruction upon me, rest assured that I shall do as much to you.

communicates.speaker: professor_moriarty

events.label: Holmes says Moriarty is his intellectual equal and would not be baffled so easily

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: My dear Watson, you evidently did not realize my meaning when I said that this man may be taken as being quite on the same intellectual plane as myself. You do not imagine that if I were the pursuer I should allow myself to be baffled by so slight an obstacle. Why, then, should you think so meanly of him?

events.label: Watson asks what Moriarty will do

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: What will he do? What would you do, then?

events.label: Holmes says he would engage a special train

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Engage a special.

events.label: Watson comments that it must be late

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: But it must be late.

events.label: Holmes says the train stops at Canterbury and that Moriarty will catch them there

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: By no means. This train stops at Canterbury; and there is always at least a quarter of an hour's delay at the boat. He will catch us there.

events.label: Watson proposes having Moriarty arrested on arrival

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: One would think that we were the criminals. Let us have him arrested on his arrival.

events.label: Holmes rejects arrest as inadmissible and says it would ruin three months' work

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It would be to ruin the work of three months. We should get the big fish, but the smaller would dart right and left out of the net. On Monday we should have them all. No, an arrest is inadmissible.

events.label: Watson asks what they should do

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: What then?

events.label: Holmes says they will get out at Canterbury and travel to the Continent by a cross-country route

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: We shall get out at Canterbury. Well, then we must make a cross-country journey to Newhaven, and so over to Dieppe. ... make our way at our leisure into Switzerland, via Luxembourg and Basle.

events.label: Holmes says Moriarty will track their luggage, wait at the depot, and then they will buy carpet-bags

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Moriarty will again do what I should do. He will get on to Paris, mark down our luggage, and wait for two days at the depôt. In the meantime we shall treat ourselves to a couple of carpet-bags...

events.label: Holmes and Watson alight at Canterbury and wait for a train
Holmes points out a rapidly approaching train on the line
Holmes says their friend has limited intelligence and would have attacked him

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There are limits, you see, to our friend's intelligence. It would have been a coup-de-maître had he deduced what I would deduce and acted accordingly. And what would he have done had he overtaken us? There cannot be the least doubt that he would have made a murderous attack upon me. It is, however, a game at which two may play. The question now is whether we should take a premature lunch here, or run our chance of starving before we reach the buffet at Newhaven.

events.label: Holmes and Watson travel to Brussels, stay two days, and move on to Strasburg
Holmes telegraphs to the London police and receives a reply at the hotel
Holmes opens the reply and throws it into the grate
Holmes exclaims that Moriarty has escaped

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I might have known it! He has escaped! Moriarty? They have secured the whole gang with the exception of him. He has given them the slip. Of course, when I had left the country there was no one to cope with him. But I did think that I had put the game in their hands. I think that you had better return to England, Watson. Because you will find me a dangerous companion now. This man's occupation is gone. He is lost if he returns to London. If I read his character right he will devote his whole energies to revenging himself upon me. He said as much in our short interview, and I fancy that he meant it. I should certainly recommend you to return to your practice.

events.label: Holmes and Watson continue their journey through Switzerland to Meiringen
Holmes watches the countryside and scans faces for danger
A rock falls beside Holmes and Watson near Daubensee
Holmes races up the ridge and looks in every direction
Holmes and Watson arrive at Meiringen and stay at the Englischer Hof
Holmes and Watson set off toward Rosenlaui with the landlord's advice
Holmes and Watson stop near the Reichenbach Falls to look down into the abyss
A Swiss lad runs along the path carrying a letter
The letter is delivered to Watson
The landlord's letter reports that an English lady has arrived and needs an English doctor

communicates.speaker: peter_steiler_elder
communicates.content: An English lady has arrived at the hotel in the last stage of consumption after a hemorrhage; she had wintered at Davos Platz, is traveling to join her friends at Lucerne, is expected to live only a few hours, and would greatly like to see an English doctor.

events.label: Watson returns to Meiringen after leaving Holmes
Watson speaks with the landlord about the letter and the sick Englishwoman

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: I trust that she is no worse? You did not write this? There is no sick Englishwoman in the hotel?

events.label: Watson runs back toward Reichenbach Falls
Watson searches the path and examines the tracks near the fall
Holmes's silver cigarette-case is found on the boulder
A square of paper flutters down from the cigarette-case
Watson unfolds the paper and finds a note addressed to him
Holmes writes the note to Watson

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: My dear Watson, I write these few lines through the courtesy of Mr. Moriarty, who awaits my convenience for the final discussion of those questions which lie between us. He has been giving me a sketch of the methods by which he avoided the English police and kept himself informed of our movements. They certainly confirm the very high opinion which I had formed of his abilities. I am pleased to think that I shall be able to free society from any further effects of his presence, though I fear that it is at a cost which will give pain to my friends, and especially, my dear Watson, to you. I have already explained to you, however, that my career had in any case reached its crisis, and that no possible conclusion to it could be more congenial to me than this. Indeed, if I may make a full confession to you, I was quite convinced that the letter from Meiringen was a hoax, and I allowed you to depart on that errand under the persuasion that some development of this sort would follow. I made every disposition of my property before leaving England, and handed it to my brother Mycroft. Pray give my greetings to Mrs. Watson, and believe me to be, my dear fellow, very sincerely yours, Sherlock Holmes.

events.label: Holmes hands his property to Mycroft before leaving England
Experts examine the end of the struggle and the missing bodies
The Swiss youth is not found again
The evidence Holmes accumulated exposes the gang's organization
The dead man's hand weighs upon the gang
The narrator states that he is compelled to make a clear statement of Moriarty's career

clues.significance: Holmes inferred that Moriarty's agents were targeting him from the sudden van attack in the street.
Holmes inferred that the falling brick was not accidental and came from a deliberate attack rather than the wind.
Holmes inferred that a planned assault was continuing from the bludgeon attack on his way to Watson.
Holmes removed the black cassock as the disguise he had been wearing.
Watson inferred Holmes had not gone to Rosenlaui from the Alpine-stock left leaning against the rock.
Watson inferred that the silver cigarette-case belonged to Holmes because it was the item used to carry by him and was found on the boulder with the paper beneath it.
